drink:Garnatxa negra and Carinyena.name: Garnatxa negra and Carinyena
drink:Garnatxa negra and Carinyena.teaser: Two black grapes off the slate, bent by the tramuntana: the red you will be poured all week
drink:Garnatxa negra and Carinyena.story: Ask for a red in Cadaqués and it will almost always be these two. Garnatxa negra, called lledoner negre on old labels, is the leading black grape of DO Empordà: warm, ripe and generous, with red fruit and a little spice. Carinyena, also called Samsó, brings the spine. Its old, low-yielding bush vines shrug off drought and keep their acidity, which stops the Garnatxa from turning heavy. Both grow on llicorella, the crumbling slate of the Pyrenean and Cap de Creus slopes, where the north wind dries the bunches. The vineyards crashed when phylloxera arrived in 1879 and have come back since through cooperatives and small estates.
drink:Garnatxa negra and Carinyena.why: Order a Garnatxa-Carinyena blend from the peninsula itself with grilled fish or a rice; the acidity carries it.
facts: Garnatxa gives ripe red fruit, warmth and spice; Carinyena gives tension, dark fruit and firm acidity
DO Empordà; Garnatxa negra (lledoner negre) and Carinyena (Samsó), often on one label together; 'vinyes velles' means old vines

Un negre de l'Empordà, Garnatxa i Carinyena. Names: Martín Faixó (Perafita and Cadac, Cadaqués), Espelt Viticultors (Vilajuïga), Vinyes dels Aspres (Cantallops). Martín Faixó and Espelt have their own cards in the larder; around €€ a bottle (seen Jun 2026)

drink:The white and grey Garnatxas.name: The white and grey Garnatxas
drink:The white and grey Garnatxas.teaser: The same grape in white and pink-grey skins: the Empordà's fresh whites and rosats come from them
drink:The white and grey Garnatxas.story: Garnatxa here is a family, not one grape. Beside the black there is Garnatxa blanca, or lledoner blanc, with green-gold berries, and Garnatxa roja or gris, the lledoner roig, whose skins turn a dusty pink-grey when ripe. That middle one is so pale in the glass that the DO Empordà counts it among its white varieties, since it is made like a white wine. Picked early, the pale Garnatxas give the fresh dry whites and rosats poured on the Cadaqués front at lunch. Left to hang and shrivel, the same grapes become the base of the Empordà's sweet Garnatxa, which has its own card.
drink:The white and grey Garnatxas.why: Ask specifically for a Garnatxa roja or gris: few other wine regions grow it, and the Empordà bottles it on its own.
facts: Blanca: white flowers, fennel, soft acidity. Roja/gris: fuller, with a light grip and a faint salinity; rosats pale, dry, red-berried
DO Empordà; Garnatxa blanca, Garnatxa roja or gris, or the Catalan lledoner blanc and lledoner roig; vi blanc or vi rosat

Un blanc de Garnatxa roja. Names: Espelt Viticultors (its Lledoner rosat), Martín Faixó (Perafita whites, Cadaqués); Empordàlia in Pau has its own card in the larder. Around €€ a bottle (seen Jun 2026)

drink:Garnatxa de l'Empordà.name: Garnatxa de l'Empordà
drink:Garnatxa de l'Empordà.teaser: Garnatxa left to raisin in sun and tramuntana, then stopped with spirit: the Empordà's dessert wine
drink:Garnatxa de l'Empordà.story: This is the old wine of the Empordà farmhouses, poured in a small glass at the end of a meal. Pale Garnatxa grapes, mostly the red-skinned roja with some white, are left to over-ripen and shrivel in the sun and the drying north wind. When the must is sweet enough, fermentation is stopped with wine spirit, so the natural sugar stays and the wine lands somewhere between 14 and 20 per cent; one Perelada bottling stops at 15. Many are then aged for years in old casks, where they go amber and turn to fig, raisin, walnut and spice.
drink:Garnatxa de l'Empordà.why: Have it with aged cheese or carquinyolis rather than a fruit dessert; a small glass is plenty.
facts: Amber to mahogany; raisin, dried fig, walnut, caramel and spice; older bottles are more oxidative
DO Empordà, Garnatxa de l'Empordà, vi dolç natural; an age statement on the long-aged ones; often 500 ml bottles
Una copa de Garnatxa de l'Empordà. Names: Celler Cooperatiu d'Espolla, Mas Estela (Estela Dolç, La Selva de Mar; its own card in the larder), Perelada. €€–€€€ for 500 ml (seen Jun 2026)

drink:Cremat.name: Cremat
drink:Cremat.teaser: Rum set alight in a clay pot with coffee beans and cinnamon, stirred until a third of it has burned away
drink:Cremat.story: Cremat means burnt, and the making is the show. Dark rum goes into a wide clay or metal pot with sugar, a cinnamon stick, a strip of lemon peel and a handful of roasted coffee beans. It is set alight and stirred with a ladle, the blue flame lifted and let fall, for about ten minutes, until roughly a third of the alcohol has burned off. Then the fire is put out with a pour of hot brewed coffee and the cremat is ladled into small cups, sweet, smoky and scalding. The rum came home in the 19th century with the Catalan ships that traded with Cuba.
drink:Cremat.why: Order it at the table for a group and let them light it in front of you; the pot is the point.
facts: Hot, sweet and smoky: burnt sugar, coffee, cinnamon and lemon, with the rum softened by the flame
Not bottled: it is made in the pot, to order, at bars and at havaneres nights
Un cremat, for the table. The Marítim Bar on the front flames it (its own card in the tables); the songs that go with it are on the Havaneres card. A glass costs € (seen Jun 2026)

drink:Ratafia.name: Ratafia
drink:Ratafia.teaser: Green walnuts steeped with herbs and spice for months: the farmhouse glass after lunch
drink:Ratafia.story: Ratafia starts with walnuts picked green, before the shell inside has hardened, and dropped into spirit. Traditionally the jars stand in the sun and the night air for around forty days. The protected IGP Ratafia Catalana asks for more: a maceration of at least three months, a herb and spice blend that must include lemon verbena, cinnamon, clove and nutmeg, and at least three months in wood. Families add their own herbs. The finished liqueur, between 24 and 30 per cent, is dark brown, sweet and slightly bitter from the walnut skins, and is drunk cool in a small glass at the end of the meal.
drink:Ratafia.why: Ask for the house ratafia: many Empordà restaurants still pour a family or village bottle, and no two taste alike.
facts: Dark brown; green walnut, clove, cinnamon and herbs; sweet, with a bitter, tannic finish
Ratafia Catalana (IGP) for the protected version; 24–30% vol.
Una ratafia, with carquinyolis if they have them. Names: small Empordà and Girona makers, such as Ratafia de l'Ermità. Around €€ for 700 ml (seen Jun 2026)

around:Figueres — the Teatre-Museu.name: Figueres, the Teatre-Museu
around:Figueres — the Teatre-Museu.teaser: The museum Dalí built for himself in his home town, and the crypt where he is buried
around:Figueres — the Teatre-Museu.story: Figueres is Dalí's birthplace, the market town of the Alt Empordà plain, and the Teatre-Museu is the monument he made for himself there: a red building crowned with eggs and a glass dome, packed with his paintings, sculpture, installations and jokes. It is also his grave. Dalí is buried in the crypt, and the stone gives his title as Marquis of Púbol, after the castle in the next card. The same ticket covers Dalí·Joies, the room of the jewels he designed. Outside July and August the museum shuts on Mondays, and timed slots sell out on weekends.
around:Figueres — the Teatre-Museu.why: Book the first slot of the day and walk straight to the crypt before the coach groups arrive.
facts: About 45 minutes by road from Cadaqués over the Pení pass via Roses; Figueres also has a train station on the Barcelona–Portbou line
Two to three hours for the museum and Dalí·Joies

around:Púbol — Gala's castle.name: Púbol, Gala's castle
around:Púbol — Gala's castle.teaser: The castle Dalí gave Gala, where he could come only if she invited him in writing
around:Púbol — Gala's castle.story: In 1969 Dalí bought a run-down medieval castle in the village of Púbol, in the Baix Empordà, and gave it to Gala on one condition of hers, as he later told it: he would visit only with a written invitation. She furnished it as her retreat, and he filled the garden with long-legged elephants. When Gala died in 1982 her body was brought here, and she lies in the crypt he designed below. Dalí moved in after her death and stayed until a fire in his bedroom in 1984 burned him and sent him back to Figueres.
around:Púbol — Gala's castle.why: Go down to Gala's crypt last, after the rooms; it is the quietest place in the whole Dalí triangle.
facts: About 1 hour 15 by road from Cadaqués via Figueres and the AP-7, then towards La Bisbal d'Empordà; Púbol is in the municipality of La Pera

Gala's crypt and the elephants in the garden; the Dalí–Horst photography show runs to 6 January 2027 (Oct 2026). around:elBulli1846, Cala Montjoi.name: elBulli1846, Cala Montjoi
around:elBulli1846, Cala Montjoi.teaser: The old elBulli in its cove, reopened as a museum of how that kitchen worked; closed until May
around:elBulli1846, Cala Montjoi.story: Since 15 June 2023 the building above Cala Montjoi has been elBulli1846, a museum and archive, not a restaurant. You walk through the old kitchen and dining room and a set of rooms laid out to explain how the team created dishes, with an audio guide on headphones, then out to the cove itself, a small bay inside the Cap de Creus natural park. The visit runs to about two and a half hours. The 2026 season ended on 12 October, so for this autumn it is a view from the road; the elBulli story is told in the food-history fold.
around:elBulli1846, Cala Montjoi.why: Book it for next season and drive the coast road from Roses for the cove as much as the rooms.
facts: About 30 minutes from Cadaqués by road, via Roses and then the narrow, winding road out to Cala Montjoi; vehicle access to the cove is restricted from 15 July to 31 August, so check how to arrive in high summer. Parking +€8.50

around:Sant Pere de Rodes.name: Sant Pere de Rodes
around:Sant Pere de Rodes.teaser: A Romanesque abbey of grey stone high on the Verdera ridge, with both gulfs below it
around:Sant Pere de Rodes.story: High on the Serra de Verdera, the Benedictine monastery of Sant Pere de Rodes looks down over El Port de la Selva and the whole north side of the cape. Its church is the heart of the visit: tall stone columns, carved capitals and a nave that feels far too big for a mountain. Around it stand the cloister and the bell tower. A path climbs on from the monastery to the castle of Sant Salvador de Verdera on the summit. The monks' claim on Cadaqués fish is a curiosity card of its own. In autumn the hours are short, and Mondays closed.
around:Sant Pere de Rodes.why: Go at opening on a clear tramuntana morning, when you can see from the Pyrenees to the Gulf of Roses.
facts: About 35 minutes by road from Cadaqués via El Port de la Selva and the climb to the car park; or on foot by the GR-92 stage (its own card)
About 2 hours; add an hour for the climb to Sant Salvador de Verdera

around:Empúries and L'Escala.name: Empúries and L'Escala
around:Empúries and L'Escala.teaser: The Greek and Roman port on the shore of the gulf, then the anchovy town next door
around:Empúries and L'Escala.story: Greek sailors landed at Empúries in the 6th century BC and built a trading town on the beach; the Romans later added their own city on the slope behind. Today the ruins run right to the sand of the Gulf of Roses: foundations, streets, mosaics, temples and cisterns among the pines, with the sea a few steps away. MAC-Empúries, part of the Archaeology Museum of Catalonia, holds the finds. A seafront path leads into L'Escala, where the same fish-salting skill turned into the anchovy trade. The salting houses have their own card in the larder, and the Costa Brava guide covers Empúries at greater length.
around:Empúries and L'Escala.why: Walk the Greek town first, then follow the shore path into L'Escala for anchovies at lunch.
facts: About 1 hour by road from Cadaqués via Roses and Castelló d'Empúries; the ruins are just north of L'Escala

The Greek town and the Roman forum. MAC-Empúries open daily 10:00–18:00 from 1 October to mid-November (14 or 15 November, listings differ); €7, reduced €5; some autumn Sundays free (Oct 2026, Empordà Turisme and Surt de Casa); check the season after mid-November
